name: Ganoderma lucidum (Reishi / Lingzhi)

lead: Reishi or lingzhi is a woody mushroom used for over two thousand years in East Asian medicine. People take it for immunity, relaxation and sleep, hoping better rest and lower stress show up as a fresher look and better skin.

Polysaccharides and triterpenes are thought to be the active constituents, with immune-modulating and antioxidant effects reported in cell and animal studies. A Cochrane review cited by Wikipedia found no good clinical evidence for cardiovascular or other medical uses owing to poor-quality research, and no trial has tested it for appearance.

paras: It is taken as tea, extract or capsules, often in the evening for winding down, or daily as an immune tonic. Users treat it as a long-term routine alongside sleep and recovery habits.

Wikipedia reports safety concerns and moderate interactions with some medicines and supplements. Product identity varies: DNA testing found many items labelled G. lucidum contained other species. It is sold as a supplement.

angle.text: Reishi is taken as tea or extract for immunity, stress and sleep: calmer evenings and better rest are hoped to show up as a fresher look and better skin. Clinical research on sleep and immunity is limited.

lead: Ganoderma lucidum, known as reishi in Japan and lingzhi in China, is a bracket fungus used for centuries in traditional East Asian medicine, in which it was regarded as a mushroom promoting health and longevity.[1][2][3] It is taken as tea, extract or capsules and is marketed in wellness and recovery circles as an immune, sleep and stress aid.

Its taxonomy is unsettled: many products and grow kits labelled G. lucidum have been found to contain other species such as G. sichuanense (G. lingzhi).[4][5] Reviews describe polysaccharides and triterpenes as principal bioactive constituents and report immunomodulatory and anticancer effects mainly in cell and animal work.[1][3][6][7]

A Cochrane review cited by Wikipedia concluded that, owing to poor-quality clinical research, there is no good evidence for use of the mushroom in cardiovascular risk or any other medical condition.[4] No trial of reishi for appearance outcomes was identified.
infobox: Reishi, lingzhi, Ganoderma lucidum / G. lingzhi
Chinese, Japanese, Korean medicine for over 2,000 years[2]

paras: The genus name was applied by Karsten in 1881, and the species had earlier been described as Boletus lucidus.[4] Molecular studies show G. lucidum is not closely related to G. sichuanense, the species often cultivated in Asia as lingzhi, and global phylogenetic work describes a complex of many species.[4][5]
One DNA-based survey reported by Wikipedia found that most grow-your-own kits and about half of dried products labelled G. lucidum actually contained G. sichuanense.[4]

Reviews list polysaccharides, triterpenoids, alkaloids and sterols among the constituents, with reported antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antiviral and immunomodulating activity in laboratory studies.[1][3][7][8] Analytical methods for the active components are an area of active work.[9]

A review of anticancer evidence noted that research is predominantly in vitro and in vivo, and called it debatable whether lingzhi is a supplement or a therapy.[6] A study in patients with advanced colorectal cancer monitored immune responses to a Ganoderma preparation.[10]

ClinicalTrials.gov lists registered trials in cancer in children (Phase 3, n=58), Parkinson's disease (Phase 2, n=360; Phase 3, n=288), rheumatoid arthritis (Phase 2, n=70), fatty liver disease, sleep quality and chronic fatigue, with several recruiting or of unknown status.[11][12][13][14] Results are not summarised in the registry entries cited here. No studies on skin, hair, face or body appearance were found.
Wikipedia reports safety concerns and moderate interactions with some medicines and supplements without specifying them.[4]
